Brent tumbled 5% to $91 this week, as recovering Gulf oil flows outweigh tanker attacks, Houthi threats and escalating geopolitical tensions.

Oil prices are set to post a 5% weekly drop as sentiment is still swayed by ample Middle Eastern barrels flowing to Asian customers. That said, none of the bullish factors of the past months have lost their relevance – Iranian drone strikes on tankers in the Hormuz are running at one clear hit per day; the Russia-Ukraine war is as frenzied as it could be and the Houthis are threatening unprecedented attacks against Saudi Arabia after Riyadh’s earlier attack on the port of Hodeidah. ICE Brent will close this week at $91 per barrel, with its trading range capped within $90-100 per barrel for as long as we don’t see President Trump’s next real move.

US Senate Backs Faster Energy Permits, Bigger Grid Bills for AI. The US Senate passed a sweeping bipartisan bill (in a 62-33 vote), four years in the making, that would expedite approvals for large energy infrastructure projects such as power plants, transmission lines and data centres for rapid AI growth.

Asian Gasoline Margins Crash to a Three-Year Low. A flurry of Chinese exports and seasonally weak demand keep on pushing gasoline cracks lower, with Asia’s benchmark Singapore crack falling to just $1 per barrel by the end of this week, down from an all-time high of $50.5 per barrel on October 1.

Russia Widens Fuel Rationing as Runs Slump. Russian refinery runs fell by 40-45% since seasonally peaking above 5 million b/d in late October after renewed Ukrainian strikes, with an increasing number of regions capping gasoline and diesel sales, hampering Moscow’s diesel export plans for December.

US Extends Iran Blockade Enforcement to STS. The US Central Command tightened its naval blockade against Iran, warning vessels receiving Iranian-loaded cargo at sea that they could face enforcement even if they never enter Iranian waters, putting remaining LPG and jet fuel shipments under greater pressure.

Putin Rules Out Energy and Black Sea Ceasefires. Russian President Vladimir Putin rejected any possibility of a ceasefire covering the energy sector or the Black Sea, citing Kyiv’s recent strikes on the Kerch bridge linking Russia with Crimea, just as an LPG tanker was sunk this week off Bulgaria.

Iran War to Accelerate Structural Demand Destruction. The International Energy Agency warned that the US-Iran war could slash global oil demand by up to 4% by 2035 if nations expedite electrification and fuel-switching measures, claiming the conflict has so far led to a supply loss of 2.8 billion barrels.

Côte d’Ivoire Fast-Tracks $7 Billion Refinery to Cut Fuel Imports. The African nation of Côte d’Ivoire announced its plan to launch a new greenfield refinery in the western town of San Pedro, aiming for processing capacity of 170,000-200,000 b/d as it seeks to reach for fuel self-sufficiency in the 2030s.

China’s Electric Truck Boom Eats into Diesel Demand. New-energy vehicles accounted for an all-time high 57% share of China’s heavy truck sales in October, well above Beijing’s 40% target for 2030, concurrently displacing 310,000 b/d of diesel demand in January–October amidst high fuel prices.

EU Pushes Methane Import Rules Back to 2029. The European Union agreed a two-year delay in the implementation of the bloc’s own 2024 methane emission regulations, shifts methane-intensity reporting into the next decade, giving suppliers more time to comply with Brussels’ stringent mandate.

Sabine Pass Expansion Clears FERC, Awaits Export Approval. The US Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) approved the 19 mtpa three-train expansion of Cheniere’s (NYSE:LNG) 33 mtpa Sabine Pass LNG plant, even though the project still needs DOE approval to export to non-FTA markets.

VLCC Rates Slide as Tankers Return to Load. Freight rates for very large crude carriers (VLCC) fell to their lowest since September as returning tonnage has eased regional discrepancies, with a voyage from the Gulf of Oman to Northeast Asia now costing only $9 per barrel, down 60% from three weeks ago.

COP31 Draft Drops Fossil-Fuel Language. The COP31 meeting in Antalya produced no breakthrough in climate change regulations as climate negotiators scrapped any reference to ending fossil fuel use, with the final draft also softening the push to lift electricity’s share of global energy use to 35% by 2035.

Japan Plans to Triple Saudi SPR Crude Storage. The Japanese government intends to lease Saudi Arabia an additional 16 million barrels in storage capacity, bringing Saudi Aramco’s total available volume to 24 million barrels, and plans to buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to replenish SPR inventories.

War-Torn South Sudan Pitches 14 Oil Blocks. South Sudan has offered 14 oil exploration blocks to international investors, seeking to lift crude output by 15% to more than 200,000 b/d by 2029, however, interest remains lukewarm as marketing the output relies on a pipeline through war-torn Sudan.

EU and UK Target 2028 Link for Carbon Markets. The European Union and the United Kingdom have agreed to link their respective emissions trading systems (ETS) from 2028, exempting each other’s goods from future CBAM payments as the British ETS is expected to appreciate by some €10 per tonne of CO2.
